As a returning Ole, I’ve noticed an uptick this fall in the amount of professors taking measures to decrease the use of electronic devices in their classrooms. A particular practice I’ve come across is professors requiring students to print out their readings rather than use a device in class to access the digital versions. This may seem like a non-issue to some, but I have many comments — or, dare I say, confessions — regarding the topic.

It’s not that I disagree with the sentiment of having physical rather than digital copies of class materials — quite the opposite. I love being able to easily annotate texts and take much-needed breaks from staring at a screen when I’m doing my homework. I share the fundamental belief with many professors and older folk that the current generation’s reliance on electronics is an extremely harmful thing. Therefore, a screen-free or low technology classroom setting is very appealing to me, and I feel that I’m able to perform better without constant digital distractions. 

The problems arise when it comes to the cost and inconvenience of being required to print out every reading for a class. As of now — the third full week of fall semester — I’ve already used up a quarter of my yearly printing money. That shouldn’t be happening. Plus, the College’s system of printers can be quite confusing to navigate — or even glitch and print your 80-page reading twice. True story, by the way — it happened to me last week. I was staring at the fifth floor library printer for what felt like at least five minutes, just watching it spit out page after page. The rest of the room was definitely watching me, too, wondering why in the world I had to interrupt their silent workspace with annoying printer noises for such an extended period of time. I will never get those painfully awkward few minutes back, nor the printing money and paper wasted.

What perhaps frustrates me the most about all of this is that there is such a simple solution to this waste of printing money, paper and sanity. Some professors require the purchase of “course packs” from the Bookstore that can be created and customized via the Print Center — and you probably know that, too, if you’ve ever taken a Spanish class at St. Olaf. These course packs are an infinitely better option than requiring students to do the printing themselves. 

I cannot stress this enough. 

The packs might very well be cheaper options in the first place, considering things like my horror story of a long reading getting printed twice, which I’m sure has to have happened to at least one other person. But even if it does end up being a bit more expensive, I’m happy to pay a few extra dollars for the organization a nicely-bound packet of readings provides. And if you’re still not sold on the idea of course packs, I’ll have you know that you can even use financial aid to purchase class materials from the Bookstore rather than taking money out of your own pocket or precious Ole Card printing balance. I seriously don’t see any downsides to this.

If any professors happen to read this column and feel called out by it, I both commend you for recognizing the value of physical materials in a digital age and urge you to take what I’ve said here into consideration. Thanks for giving my eyes a break from my laptop screen — but I really don’t want to run out of printing money before midterms.

Here at St. Olaf, we enjoy a variety of dining options to get us through the day. From the SushiRitos — now found in the C-Store, apparently — to the breakfast sandwiches at the Cage, there are many sources of sustenance across campus. However, while choices like these sustain the body, the desserts in Stav sustain the soul. They’re the perfect way to end a less-than-satisfactory meal on a high note or to brighten a difficult day. If you’re feeling a little devious, you can even pocket a few treats to enjoy back at your dorm. But what, you may wonder, is the crème de la crème of the sugary offerings in the dining hall? If you only have a moment to fight against the crowd during the dinner rush and snatch a sweet treat, what should you risk being trampled for? In my humble opinion, here are the three best desserts in Stav.

3. They may be basic, but the chocolate chip cookies at St. Olaf are pretty perfect. These cookies are immaculately textured, with a slightly crisp outside and a chewy inside, aren’t too big or too small and bear the ideal chocolate chip to cookie ratio. They’re consistently delicious, though a little safe and predictable. However, they’re a classic for a reason. I recommend them if you want something comforting, tried-and-true and nostalgic.

2. A more adventurous option, the strawberry mousse is a great palate cleanser. They’re light, refreshing and airy, making them perfect for those wanting a dessert but feeling too full for much else. On the other hand, they lack any real substance and are a little less uniform with their texture and general quality. But overall, a good strawberry mousse is a fun, tasty option that lingers on your taste buds long after your meal.

1. Without a doubt, the best dessert in Stav is… the carmelita bar! This St. Olaf delicacy can’t be beat, with its melty chocolate and chewy caramel over a hearty bed of oats. Its gooeyness and decadence create an addictive combination that you can’t help but go back for again and again. Not only are they delicious, but they are substantial enough to make for an exquisitely satisfying end to your meal. They are also reliable in their quality, so you’ll never be disappointed. Next time you visit Stav, I hope you remember my advice and grab a carmelita bar if you can!

After a year of writing for The Mess, I have yet to contribute to the “Heartbeat” column because, up until now, I have had little to say. As someone who identifies as a highly independent, feminist, and occasionally anxious-avoidant woman, I haven’t had much interest in love and dating, and I’ve enjoyed my personal freedom from boyfriends. 

With the infamous love lives of the likes of Carrie Bradshaw, Kayda from “Love Island” and Cleopatra permeating my mind, I decided to forfeit romance in exchange for sanity. Yet, over the past year, curiosity got the best of me and I started to wonder, “How bad would it be to find a Mr. Big, a Zach or a Mark Anthony?” 

Over the summer, my wishes came true, and I experienced a harrowing yet significant rite of passage — the situationship. For a blissful month and a half, I finally got to experience the fanny-flutters, racing heartbeat, and delusion that accompanies modern dating. My family, who lives on a beef farm in the boonies of North Dakota, was equally as happy and even more delusional, going as far as to suggest that “The grandkids are finally settling down.” 

Alas, aided by my inexperience and fervent hope for humanity, I was crushed by the realization that summer was ending, and my summer fling with it. I had expected something more in the finale of my first romance; a declaration of love, a jukebox serenade, or just a conversation establishing a committed relationship.  I envisioned a scene out of “Say Anything…” and was instead handed the entire plot of “He’s Just Not That Into You.” 

Fortunately, thanks to a prompt rewatch of “Sex and the City,” I got over it pretty quickly and I reminded myself of my principles. However, I’ll admit, my healing process has had its rough patches. For example, realizing that my ex-summer fling is talking to new people was hard to process. I came to this realization during one of our phone calls, when he mentioned he was leaving a party — where he met a girl. I immediately slapped my hand against my face and fought the urge to say, “Your girl is lovely, Hubbell,” before ending the call. 

Even though I fancy myself a Miranda Hobbes, who decenters men from their life and focuses on self-improvement, I can’t deny the Carrie Bradshaw in me, who yearns for meaningful companionship. I can imagine that a lot of students find this juxtaposition relatable in the era of situationships. More than anything, I need to accept that it’s okay to want both but, in the meantime, I’m completely satisfied with knowing that I will be fulfilled either way.

This past summer, Phoebe Bridgers released her long-anticipated album “Lost Weekend,” over six years after her last full solo album, “Punisher.” 

While leaning into a slightly more produced sound, “Lost Weekend” keeps Bridgers’ old style and familiar songwriting while also featuring a fresh twist. This album features an abundance of well known collaborators, including Alex G, Jack Antonoff, Bo Burnham, Cameron Winter, and of course, the other two members of her band, Boygenius, Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker. 

Bridgers’ music can generally be hard to categorize, often falling somewhere between pop, rock and folk. I feel like this album is a good representation of the range her music can take, as it even seems to push genre boundaries at times. 

The album opens with “The Outside,” a song that sounds different from almost every other Bridgers song I’ve heard. It features layered vocals fused with an ambient sound; a combination which immediately drew me into the album upon listening to it for the first time. The opening track also features odes to some of her other influences, such as Boygenius and folk rock band Sun Kil Moon.

The album also features some more upbeat songs, including the lead single “Lost Boys.” The song is a nod to “Peter Pan,” featuring lyrics like “in a twin bed, where we will all be forgiven in an instant,” and “we are born again, so who cares where we’re going.” The lyrics could be interpreted to be about wanting to escape growing up and turning to potentially harmful behavior, pretending to be in a fantasy world where repercussions don’t exist. 

Another upbeat song on the album is “Bobby,” which is an obvious dedication to her current partner, actor and musician Bo Burnham. 

In “Lost Weekend,” Bridgers does not shy away from what she is perhaps most recognized for: her dark and personal songs. “Still Standing” is about Bridgers’ dad, who passed away in 2023. The song chronicles having to let go of someone you had a complicated relationship with, but also a strong love for, featured in lyrics like “Sometimes I want you back, but not today.” 

One of my favorites on the album is “The Governor’s Waltz,” which is a song rumored to be about her breakup with Paul Mescal. The track includes one of my favorite instrumentals on the album, a distant tremolo guitar fingerpicking almost reminiscent of Elliott Smith, far away vocals, and a violin toward the end, making the song feel surreal. This is a quality Phoebe Bridgers often achieves in her music, especially in tracks like “Savior Complex” from her “Punisher” album.

One of my personal favorite songs on the album is “Haunted,” which in Bridgers’ words is about “feeling a little miserable, and going on tour with [Boygenius] and feeling so alive and happy.” “Kill Me,” another one of my favorite songs, repeats the lyric “This is gonna kill me, wait,” which could be about realizing that even though sometimes it feels like it’s the end, it doesn’t have to be. 

Continuing the theme, the song “Never Going Back” features the single lyric “Never going back again, the way it used to be is not the way that it is,” which I feel summarizes this album the best. 

I think compared to her previous albums, “Lost Weekend” gives a unique feeling of being able to get through trauma and difficult periods of life through relationships with others. While it can still be a painful process to work through what you went through, today is a new day, a new opportunity, and ultimately you aren’t going back to the dark times of your past.

 Overall, I give this album five out of five big Oles.

I think expectations can go a long way in determining how much you actually enjoy a movie. I would like to think that I went into this movie completely neutral,  but that’s not the case. No matter how hard we may try, we walk into any experience full of biases, known and unknown. 

“Resident Evil” (2026) is a horror film directed by Zach Cregger, who’s previously directed other recent horror films “Weapons”(2025) and “Barbarian.”(2022). I have to give a lot of credit to Cregger. When directing a film based on already existing Intellectual Property, and one as turbulent as a video game IP, you are burdened with the weight of every game, movie, and hope of its fans and critics alike.There’s a sort of curse around video game movies that I think is entirely deserved. If you’re going into “Resident Evil” expecting something groundbreaking, don’t. It’s a fine movie. The composition is not anything groundbreaking or revolutionary. It’s an hour and 37 minutes of movie. Nothing more, nothing less. 

Was it scary? Not really. There were some moments that inspired a feeling easily confused for fear, but more times than not the moments that really got me were from cheap and undeserving jumpscares. It’d be a disservice to the hard work that went into “Resident Evil” if I failed to mention that a lot of the effects were actually practical. Which is cool, but the lighting and framing of every scene failed to make these colossal mammoths of puppetry, goo and gore feel like anything more than computer generated and processed models. 

After reflecting on the film, I think actor Austin Abrams did a very entertaining job as the film’s main character, Bryan. However, as a character, he lacks the morals and motivation that would make him compelling to root for. Which is fine for a movie like this, but he has this way of undermining the severity of his situation.  Bryan spends most of the movie making the kind of comments I’d make during a really long shift. “I don’t believe that,” he says at one point, along with the likes of: “What is this sh*t now?,” “What the f*ck was that about?,” “Motherf*ck,” or my personal favorite: just straight up squealing. 

If you asked me if I recommend this film, I’d probably say “I guess?” It’s not even October yet, and there will definitely be better horror movies to go to, so maybe save your money for those. 

If I had to give it a rating, I would put it between a thumbs-up and thumbs-down. Right down the middle.

Aries: The sun will shine as it rises, and the moon will illuminate the dark. Just like our circadian rhythm, the night allows time to slow down and rest, while the day brings new, warm rays of sunlight. It’s a pattern the body recognizes: balmy rays hitting your face as they brighten the room, your body breaking out in a shiver as the chilly night air grazes your cheek. Why don’t you look up and count the stars before you head back home, or stay in your bed before the day takes hold? Use this time to set your intentions before entering the routine of everyday life.

Taurus: Take a deep breath in … and out. There’s so much going on in your head, a brain so deep into overdrive it’s beginning to overheat. It’s on the verge of affecting your health. Your internal systems are off their natural balance, affecting you physically, mentally and spiritually. Stop the endless cycle of burnout and place your hand on your chest. Breathe. Slowly and intentionally. Let the world keep spinning. Feel the air enter and exit, feel the ground beneath your feet and let yourself truly unwind.

Gemini: Dedicate time to a nice, long everything shower. Use that moment to truly cleanse your body. Bask in the ritual as you become attuned with your physical form. Ensure your body feels cared for and loved, whatever that means to you. Spend time selecting the right temperature, letting the water wash away all that plagues you. You must take care of your physical temple. The connection between your body and soul is deep — you must prioritize personal health in order to reach your highest self.

Cancer: Decompress. Take some time to rest. Release the tension that’s been building all day, if not for weeks. Go back to a place of comfort, change into something soft and sink into bed. Feel the pressure of all life’s stresses slowly escape while your mind drifts off. Carving out even a mere hour of your day for a moment of rest will prove fruitful. Soon you will be restored, ready to bloom yet again. 

Leo: Slow down. Ground yourself. What do you do when the world becomes too loud? What keeps you stable, rational and down-to-earth? Where would you go — where is that safe place that shields you from the stresses of this fast-paced planet? Something to fidget with or even just to feel in the palm of your hands. Something you can stare at without feeling judged. Anything that will bring ease to your mind. Nothing is too big or too small if it keeps you grounded. Let the relief and comfort seep in. 

Virgo: Stretch your limbs and allow yourself to feel blood circulate through your body. It may feel odd as it rushes all warm and fresh to sore, tender muscles, but don’t shy away. It’s one of, if not the most, important things to do for your body. After a long night’s rest, the body craves circulation. Provide yourself with a moment of movement. Let your blood make its loop before the true start of the day. This continuous stretching and movement is crucial to the body. So don’t forget to get your blood pumping; your body will thank you.

Libra: Release the tension. Lower your shoulders gently and relax your face — your brow especially. You are holding stress in your body again. Do you feel it throughout? Scan your body, locate where it’s taken hold. It’s hard to ignore once you become aware. Now that you are, take a deep breath. On every exhale, try to expel the stress from within. Feel it exit your body. The stress will happen again, and there’s no shame in that. You must simply remind yourself to release it from time to time; take notice of when your body needs a breather.

Scorpio: Allow yourself to step away from the cycle of work and go for a walk. Sitting in one place for a prolonged period of time can feel unnatural, both for the body and the mind. Work can be done later, but right now you must grant yourself a moment to simply walk away. Staying still leaves the body with stiff, cramped muscles and a wandering, cyclical mind — break the cycle and move. Reset your mind. Allow your body the freedom of movement — it allows the mind access to new ideas and possibilities.

Sagittarius: Be the first to reach out to a good friend of yours; they need it just as much as you do. We all get busy and lose ourselves in life. Maybe it’s been a while since you have planned something, even as small as a coffee meetup. But connection is rewarding. When the moment arrives and the air fills with the chatter, not a moment lost, both parties will leave with their hearts brimming with contentment. True effort is a force that bonds, bringing you closer to others as you escape busy life and dip into the quiet ease of connection. Replace chaos with true happiness, even for just an hour.

Capricorn: Stop replaying the past and start moving toward a better tomorrow. Your mind is reeling from conversations past — an argument, a bad friendship, that time you came up empty when met with an insult. But what’s done is done. All you can do is continue to grow, learn, become someone better. There is abundance in your future, but only once you let go of past hiccups will they have space to take root. Create new pathways, think of the best instead of the worst and watch your brain rewire itself until you look around and can’t believe where you are. 

Aquarius: Take a look at your surroundings. Engage your senses. More often than not, we get trapped in a loop, moving through life on autopilot and following a strict protocol. But maybe as you walk home, slow down and look at your surroundings. What do you notice? The smell of rain before it comes down? Maybe you feel its tiny droplets falling softly onto your face or the warmth traveling from your freshly brewed coffee to your hands. Is there music playing? Do you hear the birds, the chatter of people, or nothing but the gentle wind? Doesn’t it feel nice to be alive and remember that you can truly feel? You are alive. Take a moment to realize what a gift that is.

Pisces: It’s okay to treat yourself to something nice — there doesn’t need to be a reason. Get a second coffee. Get that new dessert. Add a piece to your collection. Buy that vintage shirt that’s been a grail for a minute now. Whether it’s something small that makes a hard day more bearable or something big that breaks you away from the mundane, you do not need a reason. Your enjoyment is reason enough.

Earlier this fall semester, St. Olaf Choir Conductor and Harry R. and Thora H. Tosdal Professor of Music Dr. Anton Armstrong announced his retirement after the 2027-2028 academic year. Armstrong inherited his conductor position in 1990 from his mentor Kenneth Jennings, making him the fourth in the choir’s history. Armstrong is known for transforming the choir, incorporating African American spirituals and being a creative director for the St. Olaf Christmas festival.

The Olaf Messenger sat down with Armstrong for a one-on-one Q&A about his retirement, hope for the future of the choir and reflections on his life and career.

Q: What are your plans for retirement?

A: I thought about this for a while, and I’m at peace with this decision. I’ve seen a lot of changes … When I was appointed to the position, I inherited a very healthy musical organization, the same choir, from my predecessor, my mentor, Kenneth Jennings. And that’s how I hoped to leave it to the next person who succeed[s] me. People don’t replace people. They succeed people … Each conductor opened new doors for what the St. Olaf Choir would do in terms of repertoire but also what they would do in terms of their services, community and the wider world.

Q: This is your 37th year with the choir. You’ve traveled the world; you’ve been to Australia, South Africa, and Japan, just to name a few. What does Norway being your last international tour mean to you?

A: Well, it’s my bookend. It was my first international tour in 1993. So it will bookend my career here. But the city is always beautifully adorned … The people are really wonderful. They have welcomed immigrants to their country, but they’ve done it in a wise way, in a welcoming way.

Yes, we’ve had this tie to Norway because of our founding by Norwegian immigrants. And in my position as the conductor of St. Olaf Choir, I have been privileged to encounter the royal family, especially the late king. I’ve encountered him five different times in my life … When you were in his presence, he made you feel like the most important person in the world. I want to show you a quick picture.

[Armstrong then pulled out his phone, showing a picture of the late King Harald V and himself.]

Q: What moments throughout your career specifically have stood out to you?

A: Well, I guess I have my friends from my grad school days. Right after I finished at St. Olaf, I went to the University of Illinois (Urbana-Champaign). One of my dearest and oldest friends from [University of Illinois], Scott Andre Thomas, who for many years had the choral music program at Florida State University … has become an associate artist of the London Symphony Orchestra. He would say that when we were students, I had a dream to come back here and be the conductor of [the St. Olaf] choir. I didn’t say that to too many people because I never thought St. Olaf would hire me. I was 33 when I got this job, so I was very young … I did my dissertation on the St. Olaf Choir, so I knew this place … I’ve tried to expand the repertoire that would find a place for me, the wider church of God … I’m also the artistic director of the Christmas festival, and that’s, to me, a very powerful statement of St. Olaf as a community of faith … I think what we try to do here has to be done. Christianity in this country especially has been hijacked by people. And I think St. Olaf can stand as a canon light of God’s love and God’s gratitude to all people — race, gender, sexual orientation, and identity.

Q: What do you wish for the future of St. Olaf Choir?

A: Well, I’ll say something about the choir, but also the College. I’m very proud of how this school has risen in how people understand it as a place of academic excellence. I know the three prongs we stand on, liberal arts education, global encounter, but don’t forget we are a community of faith that welcomes people of non-faith, and it gives us distinction … But at the heart, [we] are a college built out of the Christian faith. And as I said, in the best of Christianity, we are welcoming … God created people who will love songs and write ballads so that we can continue … I hope the person who [succeeds me] will recognize the responsibility to continue to preach a gospel of love and peace, and it doesn’t have to be just sacred music — it can be done with music outside of church music … A search for excellence for me personally is the highest expression of praise I give back to the Creator who gave me this.

On July 31, St. Olaf College administrators received an email from Dr. Mark J. Perry alleging discrimination in the College’s summer STEMQuest Flash Camp, a camp advertised for “rising sixth-through-ninth grade girls.” In his email, Perry claimed that due to the “no-boys-allowed” nature of the camp, St. Olaf had violated federal law under Title IX. Perry further notified administrators that he would thereby file a federal civil rights complaint against the College.

While most present-day Title IX litigation typically revolves around harassment and sexual misconduct within school programs, Perry’s complaint emphasized Title IX’s participation-focused aspects. Under the law, educational programs and activities are ineligible to receive federal funding if they exclude or otherwise discriminate against students based on sex. In his complaint, Perry gave the College the option to either “(1) termin[ate] the female-only Camp in question, (2) open the Camp in the future to all students regardless of sex, or (3) introduc[e] an equivalent boy-only STEMQuest Summer Camp that would equitably and legally accommodate all middle school students interested in STEM regardless of sex.” The College chose the second option upon the guidance of General Counsel and Vice President for Human Resources Carl Crosby Lehmann ’91. 

Filing federal civil rights complaints against colleges and universities for alleged Title IX violations is nothing new for Perry. A retired economics professor who taught at the University of Michigan-Flint for 25 years, Perry has filed over 1,200 similar complaints to numerous institutions — in almost every case highlighting alleged discrimination against boys and young men. Yet Perry does not consider himself to be a “reverse discrimination” activist. 

In a letter to the editor Perry submitted to the “Duke Chronicle,” Perry claimed that because women are “53% of Duke undergraduates,” his federal complaint regarding a scholarship Duke offered only to women was actually an effort to protect a minority group — men.

Some Title IX experts are skeptical of Perry’s use of Title IX. In an interview with Bridge Michigan, Senior Director of Safe and Inclusive Schools at the National Women’s Law Center Shiwali Patel claimed that Title IX does allow for schools to have gender-conscious programming, of which the STEMQuest Flash Camp would be an exemplar. 

“Schools have been able to create policies aimed at increasing the participation of women and girls in fields where they are underrepresented,” Patel said. Perry’s efforts to use Title IX against policies such as these, she argued, are “troubling.”

Aca Ajkoviq ’27, a mathematics and physics major, agrees with Patel’s characterization. “Who are we giving the unfair advantage to?” Ajkoviq asked in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. “I don’t see it.” 

Although Ajkoviq claims she was “lucky enough to have an established desire to pursue science since [she] was eight years old,” she pointed out that even she “started questioning things” when she saw the gender makeup of many of her STEM classes in high school. For Ajkoviq, the purpose of the STEMQuest Flash Camp was to correct systemic problems surrounding gender imbalances in STEM. According to Ajkoviq, the STEMQuest Flash Camp gave middle school girls the opportunity to “create a community … from the very beginning,” counteract common problems such as self-doubt and develop their skills in a non-judgmental space. Ajkoviq went on to say that if Perry “truly cared about sex discrimination,” he would be focusing on increasing training for schoolteachers to “address gender divides.”

Activists like Perry, however, remain unconvinced. For Perry, the fact-of-the-matter was that because St. Olaf was offering a program that restricted an activity to just girls without offering boys a similar program, the College was breaking the law and jeopardizing its federal funding. For Perry, “hav[ing] good intentions” or giving an advantage to the ‘right’ sex for the ‘right reasons’” were not valid excuses. While the College did eventually heed to Perry’s warnings and subsequent complaint by making the camp co-ed, students like Ajkoviq maintain that St. Olaf made the wrong decision. She said, “the fact that [St. Olaf administration] buried their head in the stand on this gives me way less trust and respect for them.”

Q: What position are you right now on football and track? 

A: I’m in a position where I essentially had to medically retire from football, and I’m now competing in track and field. I will be doing shot put and hammer throw this upcoming season. 

 

Q: How long have you been playing football? 

A: I started football in high school, so I did that for about seven years. I did pretty well my senior year [and] committed to St. Olaf. [I] came in with an ACL tear, so I basically had to just rehab [until] sophomore year. Junior year, I started to experience some back problems [and] discovered I had degenerative disc disease. Over the summer, I was doing some sprints and experienced a hamstring tear. So, we called in and told the coaches: “Hey, it’s looking like it’s towards the end of my football career.” However, I talked to the track and field coach, and he’s giving me a spot with track and field. I’ll be doing shot put and hammer throw this upcoming season.

 

Q: What’s a piece of advice/words of wisdom that you would pass down to future players? 

A: Track wise, do what you got to do. Keep working, essentially do what’s best for you, being able to compete at a level that these other guys are competing on. Football, like I said, I feel like it’s way more competitive. That’s dog-eat-dog there, you got to do your business. But on top of that, be able to have an edge on other people in your position. Have edges for some of these opposing teams you may play during your seasons. Like I said, do what your coach says, be consistently great at what you do, and provide some type of winning edge outside of what’s required. You should be a damn good player. Student-wise, use your resources. I believe that using your resources, being able to talk to some of the other students in your major, in your classroom, some of the professors, administrators. Everyone’s going to help you out, they want the best for you. 

 

Q: As you’re entering your senior year, what’re you going to miss about St. Olaf? What were small moments you enjoyed during your time as a student?

A: It’s been a great experience for me, really. I feel like some personal outliers may have thrown me off a bit, but I feel like it was a family here [and] on the football team here. [And] some family on the track team. They’ve been wanting me to come and compete with them for a while now, I just didn’t have the time to essentially execute what I was trying to do for them. So, I’m doing what I can now.

Family Weekend is coming up on Oct. 2 to 4. With only a few days to show your family around Northfield, here are five places and activities to add to your itinerary. 

Content Bookstore

Located in downtown Northfield, Content Bookstore is great for readers of all ages. Families can spend time perusing the shelves and looking through the store’s recommendations for their next read. Content does not only offer books — there is also a large selection of puzzles, crafts and games. There is even a large toy section for any younger family member.

Content is open Monday through Wednesday and Friday through Saturday 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., Thursdays 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sundays 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Tin Tea

Opened by St. Olaf alum Chau Truong ’24, Tin Tea is a great place to stop in for a refreshing boba drink and fresh food, including spring rolls and bánh mì. From 8 p.m. to 10 p.m., they host a happy hour with $5 drinks. The store recently introduced its fall menu, which contains drinks like the Pumpkin Cookie Butter Cà Phê and Caramel Apple Booster. “We try our best to collaborate with as many local farms and businesses as we can when we release each menu,” Truong said in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. This year, they partnered with Trump’s Orchard. 

Tin Tea is open Tuesday through Sunday 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Hideaway

For a coffee break or for lunch, head to The Hideaway Coffeehouse and Wine Bar in downtown Northfield. Its menu contains a wide range of coffee and tea, and food such as breakfast items, salads, sandwiches and paninis — including the St. Olaf 2.0 panini with chicken, tomato, arugula, onion, brie and pesto. The restaurant also sources many ingredients locally. It’s the perfect, cozy spot for a warm cup of coffee or tea on a fall day. 

Hideaway is open Friday through Tuesday 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Wednesday through Thursday 7 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. 

Thrifting

Thrifting is a popular activity among students, and Northfield has several options for families interested in vintage shopping. Clothes Closet, The Thrifty Parrot and The Bearded Mermaid offer consignment clothing. The Boho Peacock is a secondhand clothing store filled with hand-selected, stylish clothing and jewelry. Vintage Etc. and Fate Vintage carry collectibles, antiques, clothes and more. Fate Vintage also has a wide selection of charms to add to Italian charm bracelets. 

Cannon River

The Cannon River runs through Northfield and has surrounding trails to explore the area. The East River Trail is a 2.6 mile paved path connecting Dundas and downtown Northfield for hikers and bikers. Families can also walk Carleton College’s arboretum trails, which follow the Cannon River and pass through the forest. In early October, the trails show off Minnesota’s fall colors. 

Beyond these activities, families can take the time to walk around downtown and discover the local businesses that make Northfield special. 

Truong said the community’s support has been important to her experience as a business owner. “Northfield’s people are so ready to support any small business, which is really special.”

content.rendered:
When thinking about the St. Olaf Ice Arena, the first thing that comes to mind is probably not curling. This sport, where players slide stones on ice towards a target, is not widely known, especially to those living outside of Canada, but it is prominent in Minnesota, and St. Olaf has a thriving curling club team. 

At club meetings, members form teams to play matches. Throughout practice, music is always playing, adding to the fun atmosphere. At the end of each practice, an MVP of the week is chosen, who gets to select the music for the next practice. 

For club vice president Leo Barks ’27, curling was an opportunity to participate in something he normally would not.

“I started curling because I wanted to do something outside of my major’s activities,” he said in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. “I remember my dad talking about his stories doing curling whenever he lived in Alaska. So I figured, well, I will give it a try. And I’ve been here ever since.” 

The opportunity to do something new is part of what draws students to the club.

“I was like, when am I ever gonna get the chance to curl again?” said Kaia Chelgreen ’27, the club treasurer.

The curling club is welcoming to all experience levels. Students are encouraged to simply show up, and the team will help new curlers learn the basics. But for many members, curling is about more than simply learning a new sport. The club allows students to socialize while developing their skills without the pressure of a highly competitive team. “My favorite thing about curling is the low-stakes environment,” Chelgreen said. “It’s not as competitive or as high commitment as other sports. You can hang out and have fun.” 

“There’s always new people and it’s okay to be bad at it. It’s fun to be bad at something,” Hannah Yaeger ’29, a member of the club, added. “It’s very welcoming. It’s very fun. It is, again, low commitment and low stakes. It’s just a chill thing to do.”  

Club meetings take place at the St. Olaf Ice Arena on Sundays 12:30 p.m. to 1:30 p.m. If you want to learn more, reach out to club president Sam Hopkins ’29 at hopkin5@stolaf.edu or follow the curling club @stolafcurling on Instagram.

content.rendered:
Alyssa Melby, director of the St. Olaf Svoboda Center for Civic Engagement, launched a write-in campaign for the Northfield Public Schools Board of Education on Aug. 19. After four candidates filed for three open seats during the candidate filing period, two withdrew from the race, leaving a vacant seat. To fill the vacancy, Melby must receive enough write-in votes, which Northfield residents cast by printing her name on the ballot. If Melby’s write-in campaign is successful, the board will avoid appointing a member to serve temporarily, in accordance with Minnesota law. 

Melby has toyed with the idea of serving on the school board, having been asked to run in 2024, but until now, it wasn’t the right time. With incumbents Ben Miller and Jeff Quinnell running for two uncontested seats, Melby is in a strong position. 

“The community needs someone who is serious about doing this, and I didn’t want to leave a write-in to chance,” Melby said in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. 

While the sudden changes made to the ballot in early August are a cause of some excitement, Melby said she has no concerns regarding the civic stability of the Northfield community. 

“Initially the three incumbents, whose terms were up, all filed to run. I was very excited by this. It takes a lot of knowledge-building when you enter any elected position to understand the complexities of all that you’re going to run into,” Melby said. “When you have incumbents who file, there is some benefit to having this knowledge ready to go.” 

Miller, Quinnel and Melby’s combined knowledge will be especially beneficial for the upcoming term. Superintendent Tim Anderson is brand new to the position, and the district has nearly a 50% turnover rate in principal and leadership positions. The district also faces threats of nation-wide declining enrollment in K-12 schools, potentially leading to decreased state funding, which operates on a per-pupil basis. 

“When the dust settled and two of the three incumbents remained on the ballot, it seemed important we elect someone with knowledge and understanding of the complexity of the role,” Melby said. 

Melby served on Northfield Public Schools’ Legislative Action Committee for three years, where she learned about school funding mechanisms and the stress of unfunded mandates. 

Thus, maintaining financial health is one of Melby’s priorities moving forward, along with maintaining strong community engagement with families. 

“I have three kids in the school district in elementary, middle and high school, so I’m seeing the whole spectrum. While my kids have had a wonderful experience in the school district, I know that is not everyone’s experience,” Melby said. “I’m hoping to maintain the districts’ high level of community engagement by listening to parents’ concerns and considering where the board can take action.” 

On a more personal level, Melby said her final initiative is to reconsider the use of AI and technology in the classroom. 

“I have questions regarding the rapidity at which AI is infiltrating education at all levels, how we want teachers to address this and what policies we need to set at the district level to ensure ethical and appropriate usage,” Melby said. 

In her closing remarks, Melby was asked to consider the merit of building civic-mindedness at the college level. 

“Civic habits are built best when they’re built young,” Melby said. “I know both St. Olaf and Carleton College students are building their civic muscles on campus, sharing non-partisan voting resources and beyond.”

content.rendered:
Just three weeks ago, St. Olaf College proudly welcomed 3,100 students back to the Hill, including a first-year population of 850 — the largest freshman class in St. Olaf history. While much of the student body was already eager to jump into their classes, it wouldn’t have been a true St. Olaf welcome without an extravagant welcome week. 

New Student Orientation (NSO) took place over the course of five days and was full of carefully crafted experiences meant to ease newcomers into the campus community — including but not limited to scavenger hunts meant to familiarize new students with the campus, randomized student groups to develop new friendships and elaborate parties to finish off the long, hot days. 

To learn more about the process of creating a successful welcome week, The Olaf Messenger interviewed Ryan Birnesser ’27, one of two student coordinators for NSO. When asked about the importance of student input when planning the week, Birnesser said, “I think it’s super valuable. The people in NSO do great things, but also, sometimes they don’t know what it’s like to experience NSO as a student … They need perspective from people who are going to say, ‘This is gonna be a long day.’” 

Birnesser also noted that the growing class sizes did not heavily contribute to any decisions made about NSO. Several notable changes, however, were made this year for St. Olaf Orientation to Academics and Resources (SOAR) and MORE groups. 

SOAR groups are divided by the first-year seminar, writing and rhetoric, or conversation program that new students choose to take during the fall semester. The groups consist of 10 to 20 students that meet every day during orientation week and periodically for the rest of the year. 

MORE groups are more focused on connecting students based on shared interests — incoming freshmen were placed into similarly sized groups of students who reported having the same interests. SOAR groups existed in years prior, but MORE groups are a recent addition, having been introduced just last year and expanded upon in 2026. SOAR group leaders have now shifted to focusing on providing students with resources and academic support. 

Madeleine Hayden ’30 and Micah Thompson ’30 reflected on the NSO experience in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. 

“If there had been opportunities for us to be physically introduced to resources instead of just told about them, it would’ve been more helpful,” Hayden said. This critique was aimed at the construction of SOAR groups, which incorporated education about campus resources and support but may have lacked the hands-on aspect of the learning experience. 

“I didn’t find the MORE groups fun,” Thompson said, noting that there was limited opportunity to meet new people organically. 

However, both students reported overall positive experiences with NSO and the evident care that was put into crafting the experience. 

The NSO committee will continue working to develop the orientation experience for future Oles.

content.rendered:
On Sept. 19, the St. Olaf Women’s Soccer Team dominated the field in a 7-0 win against Saint Mary’s in a Minnesota Intercollegiate Athletic Conference (MIAC) game. According to a St. Olaf College Athletics game report and boxscore, this seven-goal game was the College’s highest scoring game since a 7-0 win at Bethel University on Sept. 18, 2024. 

At 12:00 in the first half of the game, Roxanne Rundle ’27 sent the ball tumbling into the net after Avery Sames ’28 and Wren Van De Walker ’27 coordinated to get the ball to Rundle. Within this half, captain Emily Johnson ’26 buried the ball home, boosting her scoring streak to seven after receiving the ball from Ashley Payne ’29. Emma Boyle ’29 wrapped up the scoring for the first half at minute 32:00. 

Twelve seconds into the second half, Johnson was assisted by Van De Walker to slot the ball home once again. This goal was not only a stunning feat, but it also placed Johnson to tie with the two Oles — Karen Schwartzbauer ’87 and Lindsey Howard ’12 — holding St. Olaf’s all-time goal-scoring chart with 39 goals. Later on in the second, Faye Leitner ’30, Piper Gravdal ’30 and Emmarie Becker ’30 upped the scoreboard with their own goals. At minute 88:00, Becker capped off the scoring with the seventh and final goal of the game, leaving the Oles with a shutout. 

Showing off her skills with two goals scored in this game, Johnson has been blazing a trail across the MIAC 2026 women’s overall statistics. She is not only holding the top slot for goals but also shots, shots on goal, game-winning goals and points. Johnson is in the lead with 14 goals, six over St. Scholastica’s Anna Marion, who currently places second. 

In an interview with The Olaf Messenger, Johnson gave insight into the team’s growing success and her thoughts on holding the top rank on the leaderboard. She expresses that her aim for success is meant for her team rather than a rank on the podium. “I obviously like scoring,” she said. “But I don’t look at the leaderboards just because I like to play for my team.” 

The team’s goal heading into the game with Saint Mary’s was “to be the loudest on the field,” Johnson said.

Johnson spoke on how this collaborative effort drives the team’s contagious energy in their competitive environment. This is an objective that the team collaborates on with Bryan Sullivan, their mental health coach from Fortitude Mental Performance. They hold open discussions as a team for an hour biweekly. These sessions have been a great influence on their team cohesion and community. 

As they continue on in the season, Johnson describes their team goal of setting the standard with each game. “We’re very resilient,” she said. “[Our mindset is] continuing to raise the level and not be complacent with [where] we’re at right now … because we will face tougher opponents.”

content.rendered:
Former Minnesota Gov. Mark Dayton recently visited the Grand Event Center in downtown Northfield as part of a tour promoting his new memoir, “Perseverance.” 

Dayton, who served two terms through 2019, was previously state auditor and a U.S. senator. As governor, he signed same-sex marriage into law, raised the minimum wage, increased taxes on top earners and worked with lawmakers to fund the Minnesota Vikings’ billion-dollar stadium. 

His memoir, released Sept. 15, looks at the events and people that shaped his political life. He was joined by longtime friend Lori Sturdevant, a Star Tribune columnist and editor of his book, for a conversation about his decades in Minnesota politics. 

Jessica Peterson White, owner of Content Bookstore, which hosted the event, said she expected strong local interest as Minnesotans look back on Dayton’s time in office and prepare for another election.

“We’re here today, those of us who are hoping to kind of learn about where to go next,” Peterson White told The Olaf Messenger. 

Dayton has largely stayed out of the spotlight in recent years. However, as he approaches 80, he has begun to think about how he will be remembered.

“If I don’t tell my story my way, somebody else will tell it their way,” Dayton said. “It [‘Perseverance’] was a chance to look back on a career.”

The book’s title comes from what former U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy told Dayton early in his career: “Perseverance is the prerequisite for success in politics.”

“I think that’s true of most things in life,” Dayton said. “I hope the people reading this get nothing else out of it. They think ‘Yeah, I got to persevere.’” 

Early in the conversation, Dayton drew parallels between his days as a Vietnam War anti-war activist at Yale University and the current political climate. At the time, former President Richard Nixon had “all the power,” Dayton said.

While Dayton now spends much of the year in Arizona for health reasons, he said he watched in horror as Operation Metro Surge devastated the place where his “heart and soul” belonged.

“Vietnam was so appalling because you saw these innocent people being maimed, attacked,” he said. “But that was Americans attacking people in another country. These were Americans attacking Americans.” 

Dayton also acknowledged that Minnesota’s current politicians have a difficult road ahead of them, with inflation on the rise and a general lack of trust in government due to recent reports of fraud in state-managed social service and Medicaid programs. 

“I think we’re going to turn this country around, [and] to do that, you got to lead upward,” Dayton said. 

Sturdevant continued, noting that “what a governor candidate says in October matters in January and February if that candidate winds up being elected.” 

“[Political candidates] got to find out: what is our common cause? What are those matters that unite us?” Dayton said. “There’s got to be uplifting.”

content.rendered:
Long weekend with Monday off

Is there really a debate to be had here? Imagine you’ve had the toughest, most insidiously long week of your life. Two papers due on Tuesday, a test on Wednesday and another on Thursday. Your backpack ripped at the strap, so you’ve been carrying around a tote bag the size of Jupiter, making your shoulder ache with the weight. Stav served nothing but pork loin. There’s nothing you could use more than a nice, relaxing weekend — maybe a day or two spent lying in bed and making up for lazy time surrendered during the week of classes. In a moment like that, what sounds better than a three day weekend — especially one with Monday off?

Friday is the ideal work day. With the promise of relaxation at the end, Friday is the day to buy yourself a treat, make those plans you’ve been meaning to, or maybe go to bed early with no obligations hanging over your head. It ties a pretty little bow on every week. Monday doesn’t work the same way; it doesn’t have the same connotation. 

Monday is the universally-acknowledged worst day of the week. With the knowledge that there’s a long week of work ahead, it is difficult to muster the motivation to roll out of bed. You might find yourself asking, “Why couldn’t the weekend be just one day longer?” The day comes with exhaustion and desperation for rest and freedom. Not to mention, it ruins the day before, too. The dread of Monday bleeds into Sunday, and all of a sudden you’re in the thick of the so-called “Sunday scaries,” enduring anticipatory anxiety. If the option was available to me, why would I suffer the symptoms of miserable Mondays when I could trade them for a dreamy Friday night? 

Sure, three days off is three days off regardless of when in the week it happens. But the feeling matters just as much as the length — if not more — and it just feels better to sleep in on a Monday than it does on a Friday. It sings promises of a short week to come; of rest and relief. A long weekend with Monday off just feels right, and it’s best to trust your gut in matters like these. Let your instincts speak to you — the answer is clear.

Long weekend with Friday off

The weekend is coming up; you’ve been looking forward to this all week. When it’s a three day weekend, are you imagining having Friday off, or Monday? I’m here to tell you that you should be imagining having Friday off.

Having Friday off gives you a headstart into the weekend. With Fridays off, you can travel home at the beginning of the weekend and have more time at your destination. Additionally, if you want to go out for one night, you won’t have to worry about having school the next day.

Fridays off from school can also be used as an extra study day to knock out your homework — or at least get a head start on it — so you can enjoy the other part of the weekend. This day could also be used to take care of any laundry or chores. 

While some students could argue that Mondays could also be used to take care of any chores or assignments, waiting until Monday to do all of it can make things more stressful. I know in the past when we’ve had Mondays off from school, some of my friends will wait until Monday to take care of all their assignments, which makes it hard for them to truly enjoy their time off. 

When you start the week knowing that you have Friday off, it makes the week feel significantly shorter and less overwhelming. I’m able to tackle my courses with more confidence and energy knowing that the end of the week is coming sooner than it usually does. When you have a Monday off, I think it makes the week feel longer. Even though it is still a day off, it just prolongs the inevitable Monday that we all dread as students.

With the rigorous workload and immense time commitment that college demands, having days off are few and valuable. Being able to get Friday off allows for students to take care of their assignments at the beginning of the weekend, have extra time to travel home and enjoy a shorter-feeling work week. 

Let’s hope that the next three day weekend we get starts on a Friday.

content.rendered:
I have not been to Skoglund’s weightroom in years, but after learning about a new machine there, I knew this was my sign to head back down the hill and check it out. Upon arrival, the gym was not very full –– the StairMasters were all occupied, a couple of treadmills taken and a handful of people using the other machines. I quickly found what I was looking for: the Booty Builder. Sitting low to the ground, with a massive strap you buckle into, it looked –– and felt –– a little humiliating to use. After setting the desired weight, you sit down, pull a strap across your hips and buckle it in. You put your feet up on a board, and proceed to lift your hips in sets. Besides feeling a little ridiculous, it was a good workout –– my thighs were definitely a little sore later. 

While I would recommend the new machine, what I hesitate about is its title: Booty Builder. I suppose it explains right away which muscles you’ll be targeting, but it also calls into question why someone might be using the machine, or going to the gym in general. It is absolutely important that we exercise –– especially as so much of our lives as students are spent sitting. But naming gym machines Booty Builder reinforces the idea that we shouldn’t be exercising because it is healthy and good, but to better sculpt ourselves into a certain look or shape that society finds attractive. With the rise of “gym culture” and bodybuilding influencers online, it is progressively easier to view the gym as one’s only means of getting in shape, and that the motivation behind it is to appear attractive –– not necessarily bad things, but based on the title of this machine, they are goals that are becoming weaponized to reinforce a certain beauty standard which is only achievable by spending multiple hours per day in the gym. 

Due to this culture, I think it is very worth noting that going to the gym is not your only option when staying fit. It’s a good way to target certain muscles and parts of your body, but simply because it’s trendy to go to the gym doesn’t mean it’s your only option. It is equally beneficial to play a sport you’re interested in, or bodybuild in different ways. Personally, I’m not much of a gym girl, but I love playing soccer and find joy in staying active this way. I also have the life goal of being able to do a handstand, so I do calisthenics to help build balance and muscle to one day accomplish that goal. I practice these because I genuinely enjoy them –– not to build my booty for others’ perception. Even if you are a gym person, lifting weights and using machines will help strengthen bones and build muscles that will increase mobility as you grow older, taking care of your body long term. What machine titles like the Booty Builder do is reinforce a beauty standard, further emphasize a trend rather than show the positive effects of the gym on your body and make you focus on how others look at you rather than on yourself. 

By all means, try out the Booty Builder the next –– or first –– time you visit Skog, but as you do, I encourage you to question why you’re doing it. And if you’re looking into other ways to move your body rather than going to the gym, there are a plethora of intramural sports and fitness classes to dive into.

After trying one of the many options of pre-made meals from the new vending machine put inside of Skoglund Athletic Center, I was definitely surprised both by the choices provided inside the dispenser and the fact that it was pretty good and filling. I finally took a look at the variety it provides yesterday, just out of curiosity. A sign close to the entrance of Skoglund points to the direction of this machine and gives a good list of options for meals: tuna tzatziki salad with feta cheese, roasted vegetable and tofu hummus wraps and a sandwich with avocado, turkey and egg white to name a few. I decided to try the chicken, turkey, bacon and ranch wrap that was $7.75. To be honest, it was quite tasty and the meal itself was filling since the wrap is pretty packed with ingredients. Although, it is unfortunate that it costs so much, no matter if it comes out of your pocket or if you pay with Ole/Flex dollars.

That’s my only criticism of the vending machine: the price. When it comes to the actual pre-made meals for student athletes, it ranges from $6.75 to $9 at most. I would assume it is because it’s a healthier, protein heavy meal for students that need a boost of energy, actually want to eat something pretty good for recovery, to satisfy hunger or just to eat something for lunch or dinner. They do have cheaper snacks like cups of strawberries, protein bars and protein drinks for around $3, which is still good for athletes that want something easier to consume that doesn’t take too much time out of their day.

The closest thing I can compare the prices to are the Cage, depending on if you also want a full meal or something small and light to eat. Otherwise, the Bookstore and the C-Store are pretty good for prices, but it’s better for students to refuel and actually eat something protein-dense, or even something small and healthy like strawberries. 

As a whole, I would only wish for the new vending machine to be a little bit cheaper, because it is a chunk of change to get a meal from. This machine offers a good alternative for a quick, on-the-go meal if you are looking for something with a higher protein content as a student athlete who is in Skoglund to practice, workout or train, instead of walking all the way to Buntrock to try and get something quick before heading all the way back down the Hill. I would also be interested in more snacks being added to the machine and wonder how long it’ll stay in operation. I hope that people will use it to get a good source of protein for their workout or just for a quick and easy meal to fill their stomachs.

content.rendered:
On the evening of Sept. 17, OleTinyDorm premiered their film showcasing Moisés Duarte’s ’27 impassioned musical talent in Viking Theater. 

Prior to the screening, OleTinyDorm worked with the Taylor Center to host a gala for attendees — complete with a red carpet, refreshments, TinyDorm backdrop, and student photographers to capture the dashing fashions of the evening. 

TinyDorm encouraged students to dress in black tie, but in an interview with The Olaf Messenger, organization member Isaac Kitange ’27 said that they could not have imagined the turnout they had received. Students arrived in decadent floor-length gowns, suits and ties. “We were pushing capacity,” Kitange said. 

The performance itself was filmed early spring of May 2026 in the St. Olaf Natural Lands, where life was reblooming after a bitter winter. Along with the typical sub-zero temperatures and unfathomable snowfall that comes with every winter, Operation Metro Surge hit Minneapolis, attempting to decimate Hispanic and Latino communities. The concept of home and safety became a question for so many people. The production became a means of defining what home is. 

The film begins with euphoric shots of the Natural Lands – geese swimming, sunlight peaking through freshly bloomed leaves — and a sweeping monologue from Duarte as he ponders what a home is, as well as why he sings; the two are intertwined, Duarte explains. “Do you know what I do when I miss home? I sing.” 

In an interview with The Olaf Messenger, Duarte said that he “would only do an [OleTinyDorm performance] if it had a social-political meaning.” When deciding on the repertoire to perform, he knew he wanted to “showcase a full Spanish set” and a “complete cultural immersion” which became an almost laughable conquest, considering the fact that there are over thirty Spanish-speaking countries. 

Additionally, he was working with jazz musicians, all of which could not speak — much less sing in — Spanish. To guide his decisions, he asked himself the question, “What does it mean to be Latino?” From there, he began to plan. He kicked the performance off with “Alma Llanera,” a Venezuelan song that Duarte believes encapsulates the nuances and power of the Latino identity. 

Following this cheerful song, Duarte switched gears and began explaining “La Maza,” a Cuban song about using our voices to speak up and speak out against repression and tyrannical power. In the film, Duarte calls upon anyone with a platform to use their voice and shout, sing and make noise against the machine. 

OleTinyDorm’s mission is to provide everyone with a platform, regardless of their musical background, and to highlight non-classical, non-academic musicianship. “No one hears this kind of music at St. Olaf,” Kitange said in an interview with The Olaf Messenger. They hope to continue to build their platform, showcase a wide range of talents, and continue the movement.

The film is now available on OleTinyDorm’s YouTube page for all to enjoy.

content.rendered:
Our world is constantly changing and adapting to things, especially in technology. One of those things, unfortunately, is the use of generative AI. 

The discussion of how AI should be used in classrooms is still up for debate by many professors, and many have decided that they personally would not allow students to ever use it. Some might even instruct a lesson by using it so students understand how ineffective and lazy it really is. 

While I have always sided against AI, my Digital Rhetoric & Literacy class led me to think about its long-term impact on us. My professor is strongly against AI, and in his syllabus, he listed the consequences of continual reliance on it in our daily lives: draining water supply and damaging the environment, rising government surveillance, breaking down people’s patience and empathy and a lack of productivity.

As a double major in film and media studies and Asian studies, a lot of the classes I take focus on history, culture, media and creating art. History is so integral in looking back on how film became revolutionized, ranging from minority groups entering the field to sparking debates on controversial subjects and censorship to local studios trying to navigate behind-the-scenes with portable equipment and low budgets. With Asian studies, I have learned more about Japan’s political milestones, including the Meiji Restoration; their language, ranging from sentence structures to connection to the Chinese language; and their cultural norms. Because these subjects are so unique, we had to rely on factual sources, which include paper files, physical books, news articles and more. If we relied on AI to help us look them up, we would lose the trust of our professors since AI has a reputation for spreading misinformation. In addition, AI steals data without acknowledging the authors. We are responsible for these actions, and we should know how to handle AI accordingly in classrooms. 

To answer the question on how AI should be handled in the classroom, I would say it should not be used at all. I reached out to a handful of my professors and some STEM students to hear their stance on this subject. Their answers were that they were personally against it, but some professors give their students the opportunity to use it so long as they cite that they did. However, if a student uses it once, chances are that they’re going to do it again and again. 

Some professors choose to go anti-technology, with no laptops or phones in the classroom due to their interference with learning and suspicions of students using AI. Professors use technology on a daily basis, and sometimes restricting it for students is a little unfair, so something I would suggest for them is to encourage students to use our library and databases for sources instead of just general research. They could even give students a broad range of academic websites that clearly and accurately cite their sources. 

Another strategy I would encourage for professors — especially for those teaching languages — are engaging simulations that give students a brief overview of why AI is not always accurate due to its generative, speedy responses. As I brought up before, professors should discuss the consequences of using generative AI with their students, such as depleting water supplies and how the rising amount of data centers being built, especially those in Faribault and Northfield, is disturbing the environment and the natural landscapes.

Imagine walking into your dorm’s laundry room on a Saturday afternoon with the plan of finishing all your laundry quickly so you can have the rest of the day to do homework or hang out with friends. Upon walking in, you see that this plan isn’t going to work out since every single machine is full. However, there is one washing machine that just finished its cycle, and the owner of the items is not there to move the load. What do you do? Don’t worry, because I’m here to tell you the proper laundry room etiquette.

Removing someone’s belongings from a laundry machine is a very delicate situation, because there is always the chance that the owner of the items could walk in while you’re actively taking out their stuff, and that would quickly become an uncomfortable situation. Despite this, I do think that in certain situations, it’s okay to remove a person’s belongings from the machines if they are not there to do it themselves. I think it solely depends on the time and day that you are doing laundry. 

On days where the laundry machines are in high demand — Friday, Saturday and Sunday — I think that if the owner of the items is not present within three to five minutes of the load finishing, their stuff can be removed. I know that three to five minutes is a short window; however, some dorms, like Ellingson, only have four sets of machines for the entire building. This means that there are not enough machines to support the high demand of laundry that needs to be done. It’s unfair to expect others to wait a significant amount of time for you to move your laundry if there’s a need for those machines. 

During the week when the machines are in use less, I would argue that you should wait 15 to 20 minutes before moving items, since there are most likely several other machines you could use at that time. 

Another important factor here is the time of day you’re trying to do laundry. If it’s a busy time of day, the grace window should be shorter than when there is less of a laundry demand. If you do plan to remove someone’s laundry after waiting the appropriate amount of time, make sure to be respectful of their belongings. Remove their items and place them into an empty laundry hamper that is available in the room. Do not just throw the items on top of the machine. 

Sharing a living space can be a challenge, especially when trying to navigate sharing places such as a laundry room with many other people. Additionally, doing laundry can be stressful when other people are not prompt with removing their stuff, so remember to set timers for your loads so you know when they’re ready, and try to be there a minute or two before the load ends. That way, you’re ready the second it’s done.

On Aug. 28, a movie finally hit the big screen that should have been there for years. A film that was scrapped in November 2023, after already being finished, was resurrected from the grave by a small, indie production studio,  finally shown to the audience who fought so hard to see it. But how did this happen? 

How could a film just disappear after all that hard work? After the storyboard and script revisions, animating and hours on sets? After all this work to create a mixed live-action and charmingly animated  “Looney Tunes” film, suddenly “Coyote vs. Acme” was simply gone.

Just like that, the film became exactly like every plan Wile E. Coyote made to catch The Roadrunner. Ending in disaster, the film dropped off the cliff of obscurity into some abyss that no one would ever see. Or so the world thought, if it wasn’t for one fan who stood outside of Warners Brothers Lot dressed up as Wile E. Coyote holding a sign that said “RELEASE ME!!”. Films and tv shows that were destroyed due to tax cut offs: This was the start of destroyed media finally seeing the light of day and winning in the fight against big movie corporations. 

Finally, after three years, the trashed film found its way home to the theater all thanks to protesting fans and an indie production company called Ketchup Entertainment. 

This was no ordinary film that was saved, but one that proved to be monumental in our age of AI taking over education, the screen, and art. “Coyote vs. Acme” showed that money isn’t what gives art value. It showed that, in the end, fans are always going to fight for real art. Art that reminds us of home, childhood, and Saturday mornings watching cartoons. The film’s story  teaches the audience that even if the original battle isn’t won, it can still cause a domino effect into something greater. 

“Coyote vs Roadrunner” is so important for the modern day. It speaks to us, and our current society. Soon, if not already, we’re going to have to start protesting to make sure art is seen, that AI isn’t the only thing ruling over our screens and that money isn’t making the decisions. We can’t forget how powerful our voices are. 

So please, if any of you have the chance to see the film before it leaves the theater, please do. It has already surpassed many of the other highest grossing films of the year like “The Odyssey” by making over 100 million dollars in domestic box office profit. But the support can’t end here. Showing up for films like this means more animation will be made, and that less of it will be shelved and replaced by AI in the future. It may not seem like a lot, but it is just one step to fixing what is breaking not only within the film industry, but our whole society.

As a returning Ole, I’ve noticed an uptick this fall in the amount of professors taking measures to decrease the use of electronic devices in their classrooms. A particular practice I’ve come across is professors requiring students to print out their readings rather than use a device in class to access the digital versions. This may seem like a non-issue to some, but I have many comments — or, dare I say, confessions — regarding the topic.

It’s not that I disagree with the sentiment of having physical rather than digital copies of class materials — quite the opposite. I love being able to easily annotate texts and take much-needed breaks from staring at a screen when I’m doing my homework. I share the fundamental belief with many professors and older folk that the current generation’s reliance on electronics is an extremely harmful thing. Therefore, a screen-free or low technology classroom setting is very appealing to me, and I feel that I’m able to perform better without constant digital distractions. 

The problems arise when it comes to the cost and inconvenience of being required to print out every reading for a class. As of now — the third full week of fall semester — I’ve already used up a quarter of my yearly printing money. That shouldn’t be happening. Plus, the College’s system of printers can be quite confusing to navigate — or even glitch and print your 80-page reading twice. True story, by the way — it happened to me last week. I was staring at the fifth floor library printer for what felt like at least five minutes, just watching it spit out page after page. The rest of the room was definitely watching me, too, wondering why in the world I had to interrupt their silent workspace with annoying printer noises for such an extended period of time. I will never get those painfully awkward few minutes back, nor the printing money and paper wasted.

What perhaps frustrates me the most about all of this is that there is such a simple solution to this waste of printing money, paper and sanity. Some professors require the purchase of “course packs” from the Bookstore that can be created and customized via the Print Center — and you probably know that, too, if you’ve ever taken a Spanish class at St. Olaf. These course packs are an infinitely better option than requiring students to do the printing themselves. 

I cannot stress this enough. 

The packs might very well be cheaper options in the first place, considering things like my horror story of a long reading getting printed twice, which I’m sure has to have happened to at least one other person. But even if it does end up being a bit more expensive, I’m happy to pay a few extra dollars for the organization a nicely-bound packet of readings provides. And if you’re still not sold on the idea of course packs, I’ll have you know that you can even use financial aid to purchase class materials from the Bookstore rather than taking money out of your own pocket or precious Ole Card printing balance. I seriously don’t see any downsides to this.

If any professors happen to read this column and feel called out by it, I both commend you for recognizing the value of physical materials in a digital age and urge you to take what I’ve said here into consideration. Thanks for giving my eyes a break from my laptop screen — but I really don’t want to run out of printing money before midterms.

Here at St. Olaf, we enjoy a variety of dining options to get us through the day. From the SushiRitos — now found in the C-Store, apparently — to the breakfast sandwiches at the Cage, there are many sources of sustenance across campus. However, while choices like these sustain the body, the desserts in Stav sustain the soul. They’re the perfect way to end a less-than-satisfactory meal on a high note or to brighten a difficult day. If you’re feeling a little devious, you can even pocket a few treats to enjoy back at your dorm. But what, you may wonder, is the crème de la crème of the sugary offerings in the dining hall? If you only have a moment to fight against the crowd during the dinner rush and snatch a sweet treat, what should you risk being trampled for? In my humble opinion, here are the three best desserts in Stav.

3. They may be basic, but the chocolate chip cookies at St. Olaf are pretty perfect. These cookies are immaculately textured, with a slightly crisp outside and a chewy inside, aren’t too big or too small and bear the ideal chocolate chip to cookie ratio. They’re consistently delicious, though a little safe and predictable. However, they’re a classic for a reason. I recommend them if you want something comforting, tried-and-true and nostalgic.

2. A more adventurous option, the strawberry mousse is a great palate cleanser. They’re light, refreshing and airy, making them perfect for those wanting a dessert but feeling too full for much else. On the other hand, they lack any real substance and are a little less uniform with their texture and general quality. But overall, a good strawberry mousse is a fun, tasty option that lingers on your taste buds long after your meal.

1. Without a doubt, the best dessert in Stav is… the carmelita bar! This St. Olaf delicacy can’t be beat, with its melty chocolate and chewy caramel over a hearty bed of oats. Its gooeyness and decadence create an addictive combination that you can’t help but go back for again and again. Not only are they delicious, but they are substantial enough to make for an exquisitely satisfying end to your meal. They are also reliable in their quality, so you’ll never be disappointed. Next time you visit Stav, I hope you remember my advice and grab a carmelita bar if you can!

After a year of writing for The Mess, I have yet to contribute to the “Heartbeat” column because, up until now, I have had little to say. As someone who identifies as a highly independent, feminist, and occasionally anxious-avoidant woman, I haven’t had much interest in love and dating, and I’ve enjoyed my personal freedom from boyfriends. 

With the infamous love lives of the likes of Carrie Bradshaw, Kayda from “Love Island” and Cleopatra permeating my mind, I decided to forfeit romance in exchange for sanity. Yet, over the past year, curiosity got the best of me and I started to wonder, “How bad would it be to find a Mr. Big, a Zach or a Mark Anthony?” 

Over the summer, my wishes came true, and I experienced a harrowing yet significant rite of passage — the situationship. For a blissful month and a half, I finally got to experience the fanny-flutters, racing heartbeat, and delusion that accompanies modern dating. My family, who lives on a beef farm in the boonies of North Dakota, was equally as happy and even more delusional, going as far as to suggest that “The grandkids are finally settling down.” 

Alas, aided by my inexperience and fervent hope for humanity, I was crushed by the realization that summer was ending, and my summer fling with it. I had expected something more in the finale of my first romance; a declaration of love, a jukebox serenade, or just a conversation establishing a committed relationship.  I envisioned a scene out of “Say Anything…” and was instead handed the entire plot of “He’s Just Not That Into You.” 

Fortunately, thanks to a prompt rewatch of “Sex and the City,” I got over it pretty quickly and I reminded myself of my principles. However, I’ll admit, my healing process has had its rough patches. For example, realizing that my ex-summer fling is talking to new people was hard to process. I came to this realization during one of our phone calls, when he mentioned he was leaving a party — where he met a girl. I immediately slapped my hand against my face and fought the urge to say, “Your girl is lovely, Hubbell,” before ending the call. 

Even though I fancy myself a Miranda Hobbes, who decenters men from their life and focuses on self-improvement, I can’t deny the Carrie Bradshaw in me, who yearns for meaningful companionship. I can imagine that a lot of students find this juxtaposition relatable in the era of situationships. More than anything, I need to accept that it’s okay to want both but, in the meantime, I’m completely satisfied with knowing that I will be fulfilled either way.
